title: Angina & heart attack
blurb: Tell angina from a heart attack, give GTN or aspirin correctly, and know what to do if chest pain turns into cardiac arrest.
question: A 62-year-old man with known angina grips his chest in the waiting room. He takes two puffs of his GTN spray, but five minutes later the pain is worse, spreading to his jaw, and he looks grey and sweaty. What has changed, and what should the team do now?

teach.body: The heart muscle gets its blood from the coronary arteries. In angina those arteries are narrowed, so when the heart works harder (exertion, stress, anxiety in the dental chair) it can't get enough oxygen and it hurts. The pain eases with rest and GTN, and the muscle isn't damaged. In a heart attack (myocardial infarction, MI) an artery becomes blocked, usually by a clot, and part of the heart muscle starts to die. The pain persists and is not relieved by GTN.

steps.label: GTN: 2 puffs under the tongue
steps.sub: Patient's own spray or the practice kit

steps.label: Not relieved, or MI signs: call 999
Aspirin 300 mg
steps.sub: Chewed or dispersed; not if allergic or under 16

teach.caption: Both are in the practice emergency drug kit (SDCEP). Many angina patients also carry their own GTN spray.

teach.body: GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) widens blood vessels, which reduces the heart's workload and improves its blood supply, so angina eases within minutes. It also lowers blood pressure and often causes a headache and flushing, which is why the patient must be sitting, never standing. Aspirin stops platelets clumping together, so it limits the clot that is blocking the artery in a heart attack. Chewing it gets it into the blood faster. Don't give it to anyone allergic to aspirin or to children under 16.

teach.text: A known angina history doesn't make every chest pain 'just angina'. If GTN hasn't worked, or the pain is worse, longer or at rest, treat it as a heart attack: call 999, then give aspirin. Don't mix up the routes: GTN goes under the tongue, aspirin is chewed.

teach.body: A heart attack can trigger cardiac arrest. If the patient becomes unresponsive and isn't breathing normally (occasional gasps don't count), shout for help, call 999 and start CPR: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, 100–120 compressions a minute, 5–6 cm deep. Get the AED, switch it on as soon as it arrives and follow its prompts. The adult basic life support lesson covers this in detail.

items: Angina: narrowed arteries, pain on exertion or stress, relieved by rest and GTN.
Heart attack: blocked artery, crushing pain often spreading to arm or jaw, grey, clammy, not relieved by GTN.
GTN: 2 puffs (400 µg each) under the tongue, patient seated; repeat after 5 minutes if pain remains.
Suspected MI: call 999, aspirin 300 mg chewed (not if allergic or under 16).
Unresponsive and not breathing normally: CPR 30:2 and AED.

summary: You can now tell angina from a heart attack, give GTN under the tongue and repeat it after 5 minutes if needed, recognise when to call 999 and give aspirin 300 mg chewed, and start CPR if the patient goes into cardiac arrest.

A.q: A patient with known angina gets chest tightness climbing the stairs to the surgery. It settles within minutes after two puffs of GTN. What is the most likely explanation?
A.why: Chest pain on exertion in a known angina patient that settles quickly with GTN fits an angina attack.

whyNot.0: A heart attack is not usually relieved by GTN.
whyNot.2: Anaphylaxis follows a trigger and causes airway, breathing or circulation problems with skin signs.
whyNot.3: Hyperventilation causes fast breathing and tingling, and doesn't respond to GTN.

A.q: How should GTN spray be given during an angina attack?
A.why: GTN is given sublingually: 2 puffs sprayed under the tongue, where it is absorbed quickly.

whyNot.0: GTN is a spray absorbed in the mouth, not swallowed.
whyNot.1: A spacer is used with an asthma inhaler, not GTN.
whyNot.2: Injection into the thigh is the route for adrenaline in anaphylaxis.

A.q: What dose of aspirin is given for a suspected heart attack, and how?
A.why: Aspirin 300 mg is chewed or dispersed in water so it reaches the blood quickly and limits clot formation.

whyNot.0: 75 mg is a typical daily preventive dose, not the emergency dose.
whyNot.1: 1 g is far above the emergency dose.
whyNot.2: Aspirin isn't given under the tongue; that's the route for GTN.

B.q: A patient has crushing central chest pain spreading to his jaw. He is grey, clammy and nauseous, and GTN hasn't helped. What is the priority?
options: Call 999 for a suspected heart attack
Lie him flat with legs raised
B.why: Pain not relieved by GTN, with greyness, sweating and nausea, suggests a heart attack: call 999 and give aspirin 300 mg.

whyNot.1: Glucose treats hypoglycaemia, not cardiac chest pain.
whyNot.2: Lying flat can make breathing harder; a conscious chest pain patient sits comfortably.
whyNot.3: Treatment must stop immediately in a medical emergency.

B.q: Why should a patient be seated before being given GTN spray?
options: It can lower the blood pressure
It speeds up the heart dangerously
B.why: GTN widens blood vessels and can drop the blood pressure, making the patient dizzy or faint if standing.

whyNot.0: GTN doesn't usually cause sleepiness; headache and flushing are typical.
whyNot.3: GTN isn't given for its heart rate effect; its main risk is low blood pressure.

B.q: Which patient with suspected heart attack should NOT be given aspirin?
options: A man who ate a meal an hour ago
A patient with a known aspirin allergy
A woman with a history of angina
B.why: Aspirin must not be given to someone allergic to it. Children under 16 also shouldn't receive it.

whyNot.0: Taking statins doesn't stop aspirin being given.
whyNot.1: A recent meal is not a reason to withhold aspirin.
whyNot.3: A history of angina is common in heart attack patients and doesn't rule out aspirin.

C.q: A patient with chest pain collapses. He doesn't respond and is only gasping occasionally. What should you do?
options: Start CPR and send for the AED
Give a second dose of aspirin
Put him in the recovery position
Give two more puffs of GTN
C.why: Unresponsive with only occasional gasps means cardiac arrest: call 999, start CPR at 30:2 and use the AED.

whyNot.1: Drugs by mouth can't be given to an unconscious patient and won't restart the heart.
whyNot.2: The recovery position is for an unconscious patient who is breathing normally; gasping isn't normal breathing.
whyNot.3: GTN won't help a heart that has stopped and can't be given safely now.

C.q: Which feature points to a heart attack rather than angina?
C.why: Angina eases with rest and GTN. Pain that persists despite GTN should be treated as a heart attack.

whyNot.0: Anxiety is a classic trigger for angina.
whyNot.1: Relief with GTN points to angina.
whyNot.2: Settling with rest points to angina.

C.q: Two puffs of GTN have been given but the angina pain is still there. How long should you wait before repeating it?
C.why: SDCEP advises repeating GTN after 5 minutes if the pain remains. Pain that still won't settle should be managed as a heart attack.

whyNot.0: One minute doesn't give the first dose time to work.
whyNot.1: Fifteen minutes delays treatment and recognition of a possible heart attack.
whyNot.3: Thirty minutes is far too long to leave cardiac pain untreated.

reteach.title: A narrowed hose and a blocked hose
reteach.question: Picture the heart's arteries as garden hoses. What's the difference between a narrowed hose and a completely blocked one?

blocks.body: In angina the hose is narrowed. Water still gets through, just not enough when you turn the tap up (exertion or stress), so the muscle complains. Rest and GTN widen things and the pain goes. In a heart attack the hose is blocked by a clot. No amount of rest or GTN opens it, and the muscle beyond the blockage begins to die. That's why aspirin, which stops the clot growing, and a 999 call are needed.

root.label: Cardiac chest pain
root.sub: Sit comfortably, GTN 2 puffs under the tongue

children.label: Angina
children.sub: Rest, monitor; dentist decides next steps

explain.body: Narrowed coronary arteries can't meet the heart's needs during exertion or stress. Tight, heavy central chest pain that eases with rest and GTN, with no lasting damage.

test.q: What usually relieves an angina attack?
test.why: Rest lowers the heart's demand and GTN widens the blood vessels, so angina eases within minutes.

whyNot.2: Lying flat with legs raised is for a faint.
whyNot.3: Salbutamol opens the airways in asthma.

explain.body: A blocked coronary artery. Crushing central chest pain, often spreading to the arm, jaw or back, not relieved by GTN, with a grey, clammy look, nausea and breathlessness. Call 999.

test.q: Which group of signs most suggests a heart attack?
test.why: Crushing chest pain with a grey, clammy appearance is typical of a heart attack.

whyNot.0: Wheeze, rash and swelling suggest anaphylaxis.
whyNot.2: Tingling and fast breathing suggest hyperventilation.
whyNot.3: Quick recovery when laid flat suggests a faint.

explain.body: GTN: 2 puffs (400 micrograms each) under the tongue, patient seated, repeat after 5 minutes. Aspirin: 300 mg chewed or dispersed for suspected heart attack, unless allergic or under 16.

test.q: Which is the correct pairing of drug and route?
test.why: GTN is sprayed under the tongue; aspirin is chewed or dispersed and swallowed.

whyNot.0: Aspirin is chewed, not placed under the tongue.
whyNot.1: GTN is a spray, not a tablet to chew.
whyNot.3: No dental emergency aspirin is injected; the thigh is for IM adrenaline.

explain.body: Unresponsive and not breathing normally means the heart has stopped. Call 999, start CPR and use the AED as soon as it arrives.

test.q: What compression-to-breath ratio is used for adult CPR?
test.why: Adult CPR uses 30 compressions to 2 rescue breaths (RCUK 2025).

whyNot.0: 15:2 is used in paediatric life support by trained staff.
whyNot.3: Five breaths are the initial rescue breaths in children, not part of the adult ratio.
